title: NVIDIA Nsight Systems
subtitle: Nsight traces are where I found what the engine was actually doing, and where I learned to check that the trace was not itself the cause.

stats.label: tokens a second on one NVIDIA Blackwell GPU at the start, 7B dense model in FP8
five-minute mean across two NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs at the end
gained by custom CUDA graphs over eager execution
slower with the key-value cache offloaded to the host

lede: Inference Fabric depended on a GPU runtime that had to stay saturated, and some of its properties could only be settled with a timeline. The runtime is a C++ layer at the NVIDIA TensorRT boundary, driven from Rust, feeding NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM for generation and raw TensorRT for hidden-state extraction. I gave its code two rules: after warm-up the decode loop allocates no memory, and it never synchronises the compute stream. The rules live in code and stop regressions; a timeline trace shows the property holds. A stray allocation or a hidden synchronisation on the hot path costs throughput on every step and disappears inside an average.
quote: "Zero allocations after warm-up" is easy to assert and easy to break in a later change, and a trace settles it.
evidence: GPU profiling (Nsight): timeline traces and gap analysis of idle time between kernels on an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU, used as proof that the decode loop allocates nothing after warm-up and never synchronises the stream.
Performance benchmarking methodology: eager execution and custom CUDA graphs captured on the same card, graphs dropped for under 1% gain, host KV-cache offload dropped at 6.8% slower.
GPU inference optimisation: part of a programme that took a 7-billion-parameter FP8 model from about 44K tokens a second on one NVIDIA Blackwell GPU to a 163K five-minute mean on two.
author: Corey James
